title: Continuatio Fragmentorum ex Adversariis mathematicis depromptorum

deep.reconstruction:
Context: fragment no. 105 (communicated via Lexell), 'Criterium pro dignoscendis radicibus rationalibus aequationum cubicarum'. The previous page reduces the cubic to x^3 = 3fx + 2g. By Cardano, x = ∛(g+√(g²−f³)) + ∛(g−√(g²−f³)). Euler argues that all three roots can be rational only if the cube roots have the shape s ± t√−3. This forces g²−f³ = −3ν², i.e. (f³−g²)/3 must be a square. He then asserts, wrongly, that the converse also holds.

This page:
(1) General verification. Take roots a, b, −a−b. Then the cubic is x³ = (a²+ab+b²)x − ab(a+b), so f = (a²+ab+b²)/3 and g = −ab(a+b)/2. Expanding gives (f³−g²)/3 = (4a⁶+12a⁵b−3a⁴b²−26a³b³−3a²b⁴+12ab⁵+4b⁶)/324. Its square root is (2a³+3a²b−3ab²−2b³)/18 = (a−b)(2a+b)(a+2b)/18. This is the root-difference product, i.e. √disc/18.
(2) Obs. I. Since f³ = g² + 3ν² is a norm from Q(√−3), f itself must be of the form m²+3n². Euler concludes that every prime factor of f is ≡ 1 mod 6 (he lists 7, 13, …, 97). So if 5, 11, 17, … divides f, the roots are not all rational.
(3) Obs. II. Uses the composition (α²+3β²)(p²+3q²) = (αp±3βq)² + 3(αq∓βp)², i.e. multiplicativity of the Eisenstein norm. The nontrivial cube is (α+β√−3)³ = (α³−9αβ²) + (3α²β−3β³)√−3. Euler reads off g = ±(α³−9αβ²), ν = ±(3α²β−3β³). He claims all roots are rational if and only if f = α²+3β² and g = ±α(α²−9β²).
(4) Obs. III. The cubic x³ = 3(α²+3β²)x + 2α(α²−9β²) has roots 2α, −α+3β, −α−3β; verified. This gives a complete two-parameter description of depressed cubics with three rational roots.
(5) Obs. IV. For z³+Pz²+Qz+R, substitute z = x − P/3. Then f = P²/9 − Q/3 and g = −P³/27 + PQ/6 − R/2. Hence 324(f³−g²)/3 = P²Q² − 4Q³ − 4P³R + 18PQR − 27R², the classical discriminant, which must be a square. All coefficients check: 1/324, 1/81, 1/81, 1/18, 1/12.
errors: Sufficiency is false. A square discriminant does not imply three rational roots. Example: x³ − 3x + 1 = 0, i.e. x³ = 3x − 1 with f = 1, g = −1/2. Then (f³−g²)/3 = 1/4 is a square, but the cubic is irreducible (a cyclic cubic, roots 2cos(2πk/9)-type). Euler's claim on the previous page ('quoties … quadratum, etiam omnes tres radices fore rationales') and the 'if and only if' in Obs. II/III are therefore wrong.

Gap in Obs. II: f³ = g² + 3ν² does not force (g, ν) to come from the cube of a single α+β√−3. Other representations exist, e.g. f = 1, g = −1/2, ν = 1/2 versus α = 1, β = 0 giving g = ±1. The correct criterion is that g + ν√−3 be a cube in Q(√−3), not merely that its norm be a cube.

Obs. I is overstated. Primes ≡ 2 mod 3 (including 2) may divide f to even powers, and 3 may divide f. Examples: roots 2, 2, −4 give f = 4; roots 3, 0, −3 give f = 3. So 'every prime factor is 6α+1' is false. Moreover f need not be an integer, e.g. roots 1, 2, −3 give f = 7/3.
The integrality issues (rational versus integral f, g) are not addressed. The next page partly patches this by rescaling.

ideas.what: All roots of a cubic rational implies its discriminant is a rational square; explicit general discriminant P²Q²−4Q³−4P³R+18PQR−27R²
ideas.modern_name: discriminant of a cubic; square discriminant ⇔ Galois group ⊆ A3
ideas.usually_credited_to: classical (Cardano/Viète background; discriminant formalised by Lagrange, Gauss, Sylvester; Galois-theoretic meaning by Galois)
ideas.where_published: Fragment published posthumously in Opera postuma I (1862); Euler's Algebra treats the casus irreducibilis but not, to my knowledge, this criterion

ideas.what: Square root of the discriminant equals the product of root differences (a−b)(2a+b)(a+2b)
Composition identity for x²+3y² and the cube of α+β√−3
ideas.modern_name: multiplicativity of the norm in Z[√−3] / Eisenstein integers
ideas.where_published: Vollständige Anleitung zur Algebra (E387/388), part II, cube of a+b√−c

ideas.what: Parametrisation of depressed cubics with three rational roots: x³ = 3(α²+3β²)x + 2α(α²−9β²), roots 2α, −α±3β
ideas.modern_name: rational parametrisation of totally split depressed cubics; rational-cube case of Cardano in the casus irreducibilis

missed.claim: Euler explicitly asserts that a square discriminant is sufficient for three rational roots, overlooking cyclic cubics such as x³−3x+1. This is a documented error in a posthumous fragment, not a missed result.
missed.quote: ut non solum praesentia criterii tres radices rationales indicet, sed etiam rationalitas radicum ipsum hoc criterium involvat
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Only of historical interest. It shows Euler conflating 'norm is a cube' with 'element is a cube' in Q(√−3), a precursor of the distinction Galois theory later clarified.

deep.surprise_reason: Standard discriminant computation plus a known parametrisation, with an incorrect converse. Nothing a specialist would find new.
transcription_corrections: Transcription matches the image essentially; the denominators '81.4' and '9.2' mean 81·4 and 9·2, and '9.36' means 9·36 = 324.
